title: Eutelsat's order book jumps to €12.1bn: why the IRIS² boost is not profit
summary: Eutelsat's order book rose to €12.1bn from €3.4bn as €8.9bn of IRIS² construction work was booked, about 3.8 times its market value. But that work is kept out of its margin targets, Eutelsat must invest €3.39bn itself, and the rest of the order book fell to €3.2bn.
sections: What happened

On 29 October 2026, after the Paris market closed, [Eutelsat](/stocks/etl) published its trading update for the quarter to 30 September. The headline was its order book: €12.1 billion, up from €3.4 billion at the end of June, because the EU's IRIS² secure connectivity constellation has entered construction and Eutelsat booked €8.9 billion of IRIS² construction work. It expects to recognise most of that between 2027 and 2031.

Eutelsat also said for the first time that access to IRIS² should bring more than €10 billion of commercial services revenue between 2032 and 2040. In return it will invest €3.39 billion between 2027 and 2034: €2.23 billion in shared infrastructure and €1.16 billion in its own commercial infrastructure.

The quarter itself was weak. Revenue from its four operating businesses fell 2.1% like for like to €278.3 million, below the €291 million analysts expected according to Reuters, as video revenue fell 17.6% while OneWeb (LEO) revenue rose 31.1% to €70.9 million. All financial targets for 2026-27 and 2028-29 were confirmed. The shares closed at about €2.01 before the release and traded at €2.00 on Tradegate that evening, so the market's full reaction comes on 30 October.
Orbit Alpha view: a bigger order book, not a bigger profit pool

On paper this is transformational. The €8.9 billion of IRIS² construction work is about 7.2 times Eutelsat's last annual revenue of €1.24 billion and about 3.8 times its market value of roughly €2.37 billion (our calculation from about 1.18 billion shares and the 29 October close of about €2.01). Spread evenly over 2027 to 2031, it would add about €1.8 billion of revenue a year, more than Eutelsat's whole business brings in today.

But three details in the release point the other way. First, Eutelsat keeps IRIS² construction out of its adjusted EBITDA margin targets. Our reading is that it does not expect this work to earn anything like the margins of its satellite services: much of the money is likely to pass through to the manufacturers building the satellites, such as Airbus and Thales Alenia Space. Second, Eutelsat has to put in €3.39 billion of its own, about 1.4 times its market value, or about €424 million a year over 2027 to 2034 on our even-spread calculation, on top of about €1 billion for 229 more OneWeb satellites. Third, the rest of the order book went backwards: excluding IRIS², it fell to about €3.2 billion from €3.4 billion in June, and fell to 2.6 years of revenue from 2.7.

sections: The real prize is the services revenue after 2032: more than €10 billion over nine years is about €1.1 billion a year, close to Eutelsat's entire revenue last year, from access to more than twice OneWeb's current capacity. Set against €3.39 billion of investment, that is roughly three euros of revenue for each euro invested, but it is revenue, not profit, and it only starts once the commercial Ku-band layer is fully operational, targeted for mid-2032. Until then, investors are being asked to fund a heavy spending programme while the old video business shrinks.

So the €12.1 billion order book says less about near-term earnings than the headline suggests. What it does show is that Eutelsat's future now rests on two European government-backed bets, OneWeb and IRIS², with funding the open question: the release gave no net debt figure and said only that Eutelsat will keep looking at ways to optimise its debt.
Why Eutelsat is doing it

Eutelsat's video business, still its largest single line at €110 million in the quarter, is declining fast. IRIS² gives it a government-anchored low Earth orbit network to grow into, sovereign European customers who want an alternative to [SpaceX](/stocks/spcx)'s Starlink, and capacity it would struggle to finance on its own. As leader of the constellation's LEO segment it designs, deploys and operates 330 satellites, with the first launches from 2029.
What it means for other space stocks

list: [SES](/stocks/sesg) leads the IRIS² medium Earth orbit segment and expects to commit up to €1.35 billion to it, according to Via Satellite. Eutelsat's numbers give investors a first sense of the scale of construction revenue partners can book, and of the funding they must find.

[OHB](/stocks/ohb) won a contract worth nearly €1 billion from SES at the end of August to build 18 MEO satellite platforms for IRIS². With the programme now in construction, that work moves from award to delivery, with first launches planned for 2029.
[SpaceX](/stocks/spcx) is the competitor IRIS² is designed to answer in Europe. A funded, government-backed rival from 2030 matters most for Starlink's government and defence sales in the EU.

sections: What to watch next

list: The share reaction on 30 October, the first trading session after the release.
Eutelsat's annual general meeting on 26 November 2026, which includes a share buyback and cancellation authority.
How fast IRIS² construction revenue builds this year from €5.1 million in the first quarter, which Eutelsat expects to rise materially.
Any refinancing or new debt to fund the €3.39 billion IRIS² commitment and the €1 billion OneWeb top-up.
Whether operating revenue reaches the €1.5 billion to €1.7 billion target for the year to June 2029, with an EBITDA margin above 60%.

faq: Why did Eutelsat's order book jump to €12.1 billion?
Because €8.9 billion of IRIS² construction work was added once the EU programme entered construction. Excluding IRIS², the order book fell to about €3.2 billion from €3.4 billion at the end of June.
Does the IRIS² backlog mean much higher profits for Eutelsat?

Not directly. Eutelsat keeps IRIS² construction out of its margin targets, which suggests much of it will pass through to satellite builders. The bigger prize is more than €10 billion of services revenue over 2032 to 2040, which needs €3.39 billion of Eutelsat's own investment first.
How big is IRIS² compared with Eutelsat's market value?

The €8.9 billion construction backlog is about 3.8 times Eutelsat's market value of roughly €2.37 billion, and its own €3.39 billion investment is about 1.4 times, on our calculation from the 29 October close.

title: FCC proposes 482 MHz more for satellite-to-phone: why SpaceX gains most
summary: On 29 October the FCC voted 3-0 to propose adding 482 MHz across eight bands to its satellite-to-phone rules, a 140% rise on today's 344 MHz. The bigger change is letting operators that own spectrum skip carrier leases, which suits SpaceX's spectrum buying more than AST SpaceMobile's partner model.
sections: What happened

At its open meeting on 29 October 2026 the FCC adopted, by 3 votes to 0, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to overhaul its Supplemental Coverage from Space (SCS) rules, the framework that lets satellite operators use mobile carriers' licensed spectrum to reach ordinary phones. It proposes raising the number of SCS bands from five to 13, adding 482 MHz, and replacing the rule that a satellite operator must lease spectrum from carriers holding every co-channel licence across an area such as the contiguous US. In a companion item the FCC also proposed auctioning 25 MHz at 1675 to 1695 MHz and 2020 to 2025 MHz for 5G, satellite-to-phone or hybrid use.

This is a proposal, not a final rule: nothing is granted until a second vote. AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile and their trade body CTIA had asked for the 2.5 GHz and 3.45 GHz bands to be dropped before the vote; the adopted item still counts all 482 MHz. By midday in New York, [SpaceX](/stocks/spcx) was down 0.8% at $144.06, while [AST SpaceMobile](/stocks/asts) was up 5.2% at $44.51.
Orbit Alpha view: the lease rule matters more than the megahertz

The 482 MHz headline is large: on the FCC's own figures, the SCS pool would rise from 344 MHz to 826 MHz, up 140%. But adding up the eight proposed bands from the draft shows that 290 MHz of the 482 MHz (60%) is the 2.5 GHz band (190 MHz) and the 3.45 GHz band (100 MHz), the two mid-band blocks the carriers want removed and which carry their 5G networks. If those go in the final rules, the gain shrinks to 192 MHz, a 56% rise. Our calculation from the band list in the FCC draft.

sections: Whatever happens to the bands, the more important proposal is who has to agree. Today a satellite operator can offer SCS only through a lease with the carrier. The FCC proposes instead a certification that the operator either has coexistence agreements with the terrestrial licence holders in the area it serves, or holds the terrestrial licences itself. The second route needs no carrier at all.

That route fits SpaceX almost exactly. The FCC has already approved the transfer of EchoStar's AWS-4, AWS-H block and unpaired AWS-3 licences to SpaceX. The H block (1915 to 1920 and 1995 to 2000 MHz) is already an SCS band and AWS-3 is one of the eight proposed. On 8 October SpaceX also agreed to buy Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz portfolio, 14 MHz of paired spectrum, still awaiting FCC approval. Under the proposed rules, those purchases would become spectrum SpaceX can serve phones on from space by itself, with custom licence areas rather than a nationwide lease.

[AST SpaceMobile](/stocks/asts) works the other way: its SCS authorisation is held jointly with Verizon, AT&T and FirstNet, so it gains from more eligible bands and fewer waivers, but it still depends on the same carriers that lobbied to cut 60% of the new spectrum. Today's share moves (SPCX down 0.8%, ASTS up 5.2%) suggest the market is reading the vote as more spectrum for everyone; the structural change in who needs a carrier is the part we think it is underweighting, though it is still only a proposal.
What it means for other space stocks

list: [Globalstar](/stocks/gsat), being bought by Amazon Leo, holds mobile-satellite (MSS) spectrum rather than carrier spectrum. The FCC asked whether to confirm that MSS bands are exclusive, which would protect that spectrum's value, but it also wants to set D2D performance requirements and said its MSS rules for the Big LEO, L-band and 2 GHz bands have not been updated in decades. Spectrum owners that do not use their bands may face tougher expectations. See our piece on [the FCC's approval of the Amazon-Globalstar deal](/articles/fcc-approves-amazon-globalstar-deal).

The proposed 25 MHz auction at 1675 to 1695 MHz and 2020 to 2025 MHz would carry a secondary SCS allocation, giving SpaceX, Amazon and AST SpaceMobile a chance to buy licences outright rather than lease them. The FCC said more than $45 billion of satellite-to-phone deals were approved by or submitted to it in the past year, a sign of how much these licences now cost.
Lynk, with Docomo, is the only other SCS authorisation holder named by the FCC; it is not a listed company covered here.

sections: What to watch next

list: Publication in the Federal Register. The draft sets comments 60 days and reply comments 90 days after publication, so even if it were published today the record could not close before about 27 January 2027 (our calculation); final rules need another vote after that.
Whether the 2.5 GHz and 3.45 GHz bands survive into the final order: that is the difference between a 140% and a 56% increase in SCS spectrum.
FCC approval of SpaceX's Grain 800 MHz purchase, and whether SpaceX files for SCS on its own licences once the rules allow.
The level of the proposed power limits at licence boundaries, which decides how usable the shared bands are next to carriers' 5G networks.

faq: Did the FCC give SpaceX more spectrum on 29 October?

No. It adopted a proposal that seeks comment on adding 482 MHz to the satellite-to-phone (SCS) framework. Nothing is granted until a final order, and the record cannot close before late January 2027 at the earliest on the FCC's 60 and 90 day comment timetable.
Why do AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile oppose it?

They say satellite signals in the 2.5 GHz and 3.45 GHz bands could interfere with 5G networks serving more than 300 million people. Those two bands are 290 MHz, or 60%, of the 482 MHz proposed, by our addition of the FCC's band list.
Is this better for SpaceX or AST SpaceMobile?

Both get more eligible bands. The proposal to let an operator that holds the terrestrial licences itself skip the carrier lease helps SpaceX more, because it has bought H block, AWS-3 and (pending) 800 MHz licences. AST SpaceMobile's authorisation is shared with Verizon, AT&T and FirstNet, so it still relies on carrier agreement.

title: SpaceX's $40B Apollo GPU lease: debt doubles, $2B a quarter from 2027
summary: SpaceX has committed to a $40 billion, five-year finance lease of Nvidia GPUs from an Apollo-managed lessor. Our calculation: debt and leases roughly double to $79 billion, and principal alone runs at about $2 billion a quarter once the chips arrive, nearly five times the AI unit's Q3 operating profit.
sections: What happened

On 24 October 2026 SpaceX signed a binding commitment letter for a master finance lease with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, and disclosed it in an 8-K on 26 October. The lessor will buy GPU pods and related equipment and lease them to SpaceX in tranches, each for about five to five and a quarter years. SpaceX expects total principal payments of about $40 billion. SpaceX says the chips are Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin, for its ground-based compute buildout.

Rent is paid quarterly in advance: one-twentieth of each tranche's cost, plus interest at a fixed rate still to be set at pricing, plus ongoing costs. The lease is expected to close before the end of 2026, and payments start as GPUs are delivered in the first half of 2027. Goldman Sachs structured it, with BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR-advised accounts among the anchor investors.

The share reaction was small. [SPCX](/stocks/spcx) closed at $146.90 on 26 October, 0.4% below the previous close, rose 1.1% to $148.58 on 27 October and fell 2.3% to $145.23 on 28 October. Talks on a $40 billion Apollo-led chip financing had been reported as early as 7 October, so the size was not a surprise.
Orbit Alpha view: cheap money, but the chips must pay $2B a quarter

The headline is the size. The more useful number is the repayment speed. Because each tranche repays one-twentieth of its cost every quarter, the whole $40 billion is repaid over about five years. Once all tranches are delivered, that is about $2 billion of principal every quarter, or $8 billion a year, before interest.

sections: Our working: debt and finance leases were $38.99 billion at 30 September, from the 10-Q, so adding $40 billion gives about $79 billion. Scheduled principal for 2028 and 2029 comes from the 10-Q maturity table. The interest rate has not been set, so we use 6% purely to show scale: first-year interest on a balance falling from $38 billion to $32 billion is about $2.1 billion, against $675 million of total interest expense in Q3. Each percentage point on the final rate adds about $0.95 billion over the life of the lease. Market value uses 13.58 billion shares outstanding on 15 October and the $145.23 close on 28 October.

Set against SpaceX's equity value, the extra debt is small: about 4% of market value even after the lease. Set against what the AI business earns today, it is large. The Super Intelligence segment made $431 million of operating income in Q3 on $7.56 billion of revenue. The lease alone will need about $2 billion of principal a quarter, nearly five times that figure, plus interest. The finance chief says SpaceX sees payback of less than a year on AI infrastructure. If that holds, the new chips cover their rent easily; if GPU rental prices fall, Starlink has to carry it. Connectivity made $2.37 billion of operating income in Q3, so the lease principal would take about 85% of a quarter of today's Starlink profit.

Two features shift risk to SpaceX shareholders. First, this is a finance lease that repays the full cost over five years, so SpaceX carries the risk that the Vera Rubin chips lose earning power before they are paid off, for example when a newer chip generation arrives. Second, payments are fixed and quarterly whatever AI demand does in 2028 to 2032.
Why SpaceX did it

Cash is going out much faster than it comes in. In the first nine months of 2026 SpaceX generated $13.1 billion from operations but spent $48.1 billion on property and equipment, a gap of about $35 billion. It guided to $35 billion to $40 billion of capital spending in Q4 alone, against $89.9 billion of cash and marketable securities at 30 September. On our calculation, Q4 spending at that guidance would take the pile down to roughly $50 billion to $55 billion before Q4 operating cash flow. The lease moves an amount equal to 83% of the nine-month equipment spend off the upfront cash line and spreads it over five years.

It also widens who funds the AI buildout. Until now SpaceX's AI hardware leases have come from Valor Equity Partners, a related party whose founder sits on the SpaceX board: those obligations grew from $4.5 billion at the end of 2025 to $12.9 billion at 30 September and made up $351 million of Q3's $675 million interest expense. The Apollo lease is about three times that size and comes from outside lenders, which the finance chief described as diversifying funding sources.
What it means for other space stocks

list: Scale: the $40 billion lease is larger than the whole market value of [Rocket Lab](/stocks/rklb), about $36.8 billion at its 28 October close of $58.60. SpaceX's AI spending now dwarfs the space sector it is listed in.

SpaceX's capital is going to compute, not rockets: of $19.6 billion of Q3 capital spending, $16.4 billion went to AI, while the Space segment lost $7 million. For investors who own SPCX as a space stock, more of the result now depends on GPU economics. See the [SpaceX Q3 results](/results/spcx-q3-2026).

Lenders are willing to fund this kind of build at scale when strong cash flows sit behind it. Smaller companies with heavy satellite spending, such as [AST SpaceMobile](/stocks/asts), do not have a Starlink-sized earner behind their borrowing, so this deal is not a template they can copy on the same terms.

sections: What to watch next

list: The fixed rate, set at pricing before the master lease is signed, and the closing, expected before the end of 2026.
GPU deliveries in the first half of 2027, which start the quarterly payments.
AI segment operating income in the Q4 and Q1 results against the roughly $2 billion of quarterly principal to come. SpaceX has guided to Q1 2027 revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion.

The 8 December lock-up expiry and the Tesla merger talks, which also bear on the share price. See [when the SpaceX lock-up ends](/articles/spacex-lock-up-ends-8-december) and [are SpaceX and Tesla merging?](/articles/are-spacex-and-tesla-merging).

faq: How much will SpaceX pay each year under the Apollo GPU lease?

About $8 billion a year of principal once all tranches are delivered, because each quarterly payment repays one-twentieth of a tranche's cost. Interest comes on top at a fixed rate not yet set. At an illustrative 6% rate, our calculation puts first-year interest at about $2.1 billion.
Does the lease make SpaceX highly indebted?

Not against its size. Debt and finance leases roughly double from $39.0 billion to about $79 billion, but that is about 4% of SpaceX's market value of roughly $1.97 trillion at the 28 October close. The pressure is on cash flow: the lease needs about $2 billion a quarter, while the AI segment made $431 million of operating income in Q3.
Why lease the GPUs instead of buying them with cash?

SpaceX spent $48.1 billion on equipment in the first nine months of 2026 against $13.1 billion of operating cash flow, and guided to $35 billion to $40 billion more in Q4. Leasing spreads $40 billion of chip costs over five years and adds lenders beyond Valor Equity Partners, a related party.

title: FCC clears Amazon-Globalstar deal: why GSAT still trades below $90
summary: The FCC approved Amazon Leo's $11.5 billion Globalstar purchase on 27 October. The headline price is $90, but with Amazon at $254.60 the stock option is worth $81.73 and cash is capped at 40%, so the realistic mix is worth about $85.04, close to GSAT's $84.07 close.
sections: What happened

On 27 October 2026 the FCC's Space Bureau approved Amazon Leo's application to acquire about 25 megahertz of Globalstar's internationally harmonised mobile-satellite spectrum. The FCC said this concludes its review of the $11.5 billion purchase, finding the deal likely to improve coverage in unserved areas and strengthen emergency communications, with no material harm to the public interest.
Globalstar closed at $83.90 that day, up 1.2%, on about 2.1 million shares, roughly three times recent volume. It closed at $84.07 on 28 October.
Orbit Alpha view: the $90 headline is not the real price

Each Globalstar share can be swapped for $90 in cash or 0.3210 Amazon shares, but the stock option is only capped at $90, not guaranteed. It reaches $90 only if Amazon trades at about $280.37 or higher. At Amazon's 28 October close of $254.60, 0.3210 shares were worth $81.73.

Cash is limited to 40% of all Globalstar shares. With the stock option worth less than $90, holders have every reason to ask for cash, and if they all do, each is paid roughly 40% in cash and 60% in Amazon stock. That mix was worth about $85.04 on 28 October, only about 1.1% above Globalstar's $84.07 close, not the 7% gap the $90 headline suggests.

In short, the market is pricing Globalstar as a share in Amazon with a cash cushion, not as a $90 cash takeover. Until the deal closes, Globalstar's price will move with Amazon's: every $10 move in Amazon shifts the blended value by about $1.93 a share. These figures are our own calculations from the published terms and closing prices, and the final split depends on what holders actually elect.
Why Amazon is paying $11.5 billion

Spectrum is the scarce asset in phone-to-satellite service. Globalstar brings about 25 megahertz of mobile-satellite spectrum that is harmonised internationally, a working constellation, and Apple as an existing customer for iPhone and Apple Watch satellite features. Amazon has said its own direct-to-device satellites start deploying in 2028, so buying Globalstar gives Amazon Leo a spectrum position and a paying customer years before its own system is in orbit.

It also turns the phone-to-satellite race into three well-funded players in the US: SpaceX, which the FCC said holds an authorisation for a 15,000-satellite direct-to-device constellation, [AST SpaceMobile](/stocks/asts) with a 248-satellite authorisation, and now Amazon with Globalstar's spectrum and the Apple relationship.
What it means for other space stocks

list: [MDA Space](/stocks/mda) is building Globalstar's next satellites, and hitting milestones on those replacement satellites is a condition of the deal closing. Amazon has said it will keep supporting the Apple service on those satellites, which points to the programme continuing under new ownership.

[AST SpaceMobile](/stocks/asts) now faces Amazon's balance sheet in the race to sign mobile network operators, alongside SpaceX. The FCC's 29 October vote on new spectrum for direct-to-device services matters for all three.
Globalstar holders who take Amazon stock become Amazon shareholders, so after closing GSAT stops being a pure-play space stock.

sections: What to watch next

list: Amazon's share price against about $280.37, the level at which the stock option is worth the full $90.

Progress on Globalstar's replacement satellites, a closing condition, and any use of the up to $110 million downward price adjustment, which is roughly $0.85 per Globalstar share based on a market value of about $10.9 billion.
The election deadline and proration result once Amazon's registration statement is effective; closing is expected in 2027.
Follow the live price on the [GSAT stock page](/stocks/gsat).

faq: Will Globalstar shareholders get $90 a share?

Not necessarily. $90 is the cash price, but cash is capped at 40% of shares. The rest is paid in Amazon stock at 0.3210 shares each, which was worth $81.73 at Amazon's 28 October close. Holders who elect cash are likely to receive a mix of the two.
Is the Amazon Globalstar deal finished?
No. The FCC has completed its review, but closing is expected in 2027, once remaining conditions are met, including milestones on Globalstar's replacement satellites.
Will iPhone Emergency SOS keep working?
Yes, according to Amazon and Apple. Amazon Leo will continue to support iPhone and Apple Watch models that use Globalstar's satellites today.

title: Are SpaceX and Tesla merging?
summary: Not yet. On 20 October 2026 Elon Musk said SpaceX and Tesla had each formed a special committee of independent directors to consider a merger, but no terms have been agreed. A deal would need approval from both committees and boards, Musk as SpaceX's controlling shareholder, and 50% of all Tesla shares.
sections: The short answer

There is no merger agreement. On SpaceX's Q3 2026 results call on Tuesday 20 October, Musk said the boards of SpaceX and Tesla had each set up a special committee of independent directors to look at combining the two companies. He said the committees were formed at shareholders' request and had not agreed any terms.

Musk said he thought a merger would be "a good idea" but that calling it a certainty would be "overstating it", and that "the shareholders have to be supportive of this". Because he runs and is the largest individual shareholder of both companies, he said he is a conflicted party and cannot take part in the committees' discussions.
In its quarterly filing on Thursday 22 October, SpaceX said: "No determination by our special committee has been made regarding any potential combination."

sections: The voting maths differs sharply between the two companies. Musk controls SpaceX through 10-vote shares, with almost 80% of the voting power according to CNBC, and SpaceX is a "controlled company" under Nasdaq rules, as its IPO prospectus explains. At Tesla, he beneficially owns 19.8% of the shares according to its latest proxy filing.
How a deal could be structured

Neither company has announced a structure. According to Reuters, citing people familiar with the talks, both sides have hired advisers but discussions are at an early stage. The options include SpaceX buying Tesla or the two combining under a new holding company, and an all-stock deal is among the ways of paying being considered.
SpaceX is valued at around $2 trillion and Tesla at around $1.5 trillion, so a combination would be the largest merger on record. Reuters described it as a potential $3.5 trillion deal.

The companies already work together. They are building the Terafab chip plant in Texas with Intel, and Tesla's new Roadster was developed with SpaceX technology. Musk has combined his companies before: SpaceX acquired xAI in February 2026, in a deal that valued the combined group at $1.25 trillion.
Timing

No timetable has been announced. Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that there is a push to announce a deal in the first half of 2027. Reuters reported on 22 October that some insiders worried Musk's public comments could invite shareholder scrutiny and delay the process by several weeks.
Tesla did not add anything on its own Q3 call on 21 October. Musk said: "I think I said everything that should be said yesterday."
How SPCX has traded

SPCX rose on Wednesday 21 October after Q3 results and the merger comments, then fell 9% on Thursday 22 October, according to CNBC. That was also the day up to 1.3 billion locked-up shares became free to sell; the [SpaceX lockup calendar](/spacex-stock/lockup-calendar) has every release and the move on each day.

For the quarter itself, see the [SpaceX Q3 2026 results](/results/spcx-q3-2026), and for the next big unlock, [when the SpaceX lock-up ends on 8 December](/articles/spacex-lock-up-ends-8-december). The [SPCX stock page](/stocks/spcx) has the live price and filings.
faq: Has a SpaceX and Tesla merger been agreed?

No. Both companies have formed special committees of independent directors to consider a merger, but no terms have been agreed and SpaceX said on 22 October that its committee had made no determination.
Does Elon Musk get a vote on a SpaceX and Tesla merger?
Yes, at SpaceX. Musk says he is staying out of the committee talks, but SpaceX's filing says any combination would need the approval of its controlling shareholder, which is Musk.
What would Tesla shareholders need to approve?
Musk said a deal would need a vote of 50% of all Tesla shares, not just those that vote. He beneficially owns 19.8% of Tesla.
When could a SpaceX and Tesla merger be announced?
There is no official timetable. Bloomberg reported a push to announce a deal in the first half of 2027.

title: Will SpaceX join the S&P 500?
summary: Not before June 2027. The S&P 500 requires 12 months of trading after an IPO, and SpaceX listed on 12 June 2026. It must also show positive GAAP earnings in its latest quarter and over its last four quarters combined, and S&P decided in June 2026 not to fast-track very large IPOs.
sections: The short answer

SpaceX is not in the S&P 500 and cannot join before June 2027. The index only considers companies that have traded for at least 12 months after their IPO, and SpaceX started trading on Nasdaq on 12 June 2026. Even then, it has to pass the index's profitability and float tests, and the final decision rests with S&P's Index Committee.
SpaceX is already in the Nasdaq-100, which it joined in July 2026 under a fast-entry rule Nasdaq added in May 2026.

sections: Profitability is the open question

Q3 2026 was SpaceX's first profitable quarter as a listed company: net income of $4.40B on revenue of $14.58B. About $1.61B of that came from below the operating line (other income, net interest income and a tax benefit), and management said fourth-quarter gross margins should normalise after one-time benefits in Q3.

For a review in mid-2027, the four quarters that count would most likely run from Q2 2026 to Q1 2027. The two reported so far add up to a profit of about $3.86B: a net loss of $541M in Q2 2026, from SpaceX's 10-Q, and net income of $4.40B in Q3. SpaceX would then need Q1 2027 itself to be profitable and the four-quarter total to stay positive.
See the [SpaceX Q3 2026 results](/results/spcx-q3-2026) for the full numbers.
S&P decided not to change the rules

S&P Dow Jones Indices consulted in 2026 on whether to change how very large new listings enter its US indices. On 4 June 2026 it announced no changes to the S&P 500 methodology, so there is no fast-entry route for mega-cap IPOs.

The Nasdaq-100 took the opposite approach. Since May 2026, a new listing whose full market value would rank in the index's top 40 can skip the usual three-month wait, which is how SpaceX joined it within weeks of its IPO.
What inclusion would mean

When a company joins the S&P 500, funds that track the index have to buy its shares in proportion to its float-adjusted market value. That buying is why index additions are closely watched. For SpaceX, the float adjustment matters: only freely tradable shares count, so the weight would be well below its full market value while Elon Musk and other insiders hold most of the stock.
Until then, the main dates for SPCX holders are the remaining lock-up releases: see the [SpaceX lockup calendar](/spacex-stock/lockup-calendar).
faq: Is SpaceX in the S&P 500?
No. SpaceX is not in the S&P 500. It is in the Nasdaq-100, which it joined in July 2026.
When could SpaceX be added to the S&P 500?
June 2027 at the earliest, once it has traded for 12 months, and only if it also passes the profitability and float tests and the Index Committee selects it.
Why didn't SpaceX join the S&P 500 straight away?
The S&P 500 has no fast-entry rule for new listings. S&P consulted on adding one and announced on 4 June 2026 that it would not change the S&P 500 methodology.
Is SpaceX profitable?
It made net income of $4.40B in Q3 2026, its first profit as a listed company, but a net loss of $413M over the first nine months of 2026.

title: What happens when SpaceX's lock-up ends on 8 December?
summary: On Tuesday 8 December 2026 SpaceX's main 180-day lock-up ends, freeing about 798 million remaining shares held by employees and early investors. The last release before that, of up to 328.4 million shares on Monday 26 October, saw SPCX close 0.4% lower. Elon Musk's own lock-up runs until June 2027.
sections: What unlocks on 8 December

8 December 2026 is day 180 after SpaceX priced its IPO on 11 June, when the main lock-up covering employees and most pre-IPO investors expires. About 798 million shares, the remaining 17% of that pool, become free to sell. The figure is approximate because each holder's release depends on what they held.
Musk and the largest holders are not part of this release. They agreed to a separate, longer lock-up.
The last release before 8 December

Day 135 fell on Saturday 24 October, so up to 328.4 million shares became free from the start of trading on Monday 26 October. SPCX closed at $146.90 that day, down 0.4% from $147.49 on Friday 23 October. That was the last release before 8 December.

sections: The reaction has been mixed. The largest release so far, on 22 October, brought the biggest fall, a day after the shares rose about 8% on Q3 results. The 26 October release brought a small fall of 0.4%. Across the releases the stock has still risen: from around $108 before the first one to about $145 after the 22 October release and $146.90 after the 26 October one.
Every date, share count and daily move is on the [SpaceX lockup calendar](/spacex-stock/lockup-calendar).
Why lock-up releases can move the price

list: Supply: a release adds shares that can be sold, and traders often position for that in the days before a large one.
Choice: how much is actually sold depends on holders. Employees may sell to diversify; long-term investors may hold.
Visibility: directors and officers report sales on Form 4 within two business days, but most employees and smaller investors do not file, so trading volume on the day is the better guide.

sections: What comes after 8 December

Musk and a group of large shareholders, together holding about 7.8 billion shares, are under an extended lock-up that releases in stages tied to SpaceX's results from Q4 2026 to Q2 2027. Musk himself cannot sell before June 2027. The full schedule is on the [lockup calendar](/spacex-stock/lockup-calendar).
faq: How many SpaceX shares unlock on 8 December?
About 798 million, the remaining 17% of the main lock-up pool held by employees and early investors.
When is the next SpaceX unlock?

Tuesday 8 December 2026, when the main lock-up ends and about 798 million remaining shares become free to sell. The previous release, of up to 328.4 million shares on 26 October (day 135), saw SPCX close 0.4% lower.
Can Elon Musk sell SpaceX shares after 8 December?
No. Musk is under a separate 366-day lock-up and cannot sell before June 2027.
What happened to SPCX on the last big unlock?
On 22 October 2026, when up to 1.3 billion shares were released, SPCX fell about 9%, a day after rising about 8% on Q3 results.

title: When does Rocket Lab report Q3 2026 earnings?
summary: Rocket Lab reports Q3 2026 results after the US market close on Monday 9 November 2026, with a call at 5pm Eastern (10pm UK). It has guided to revenue of $250M to $265M, after a record $234M in Q2, and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $17M to $23M.
sections: The date

Rocket Lab announced on 20 October 2026 that it will publish third-quarter 2026 results after the US market close on Monday 9 November 2026. The conference call starts at 2pm Pacific, 5pm Eastern and 10pm UK time, with a webcast on Rocket Lab's investor relations website.
Some earnings calendars showed an earlier projected date of 6 November; the company's own announcement is the one to go by.
What Rocket Lab has guided
Q2 revenue was a record, and the guidance points to another record quarter. Margins and adjusted EBITDA were guided lower than in Q2.
What to watch

list: Revenue against the $250M to $265M range.
Backlog, which was a record $2.36B at the end of Q2, up 137% on a year earlier.
Neutron: in August Rocket Lab said Stage 1 tank production was aligned with delivering Neutron to the launch pad in Q4 2026. Any update on the first launch date.
Iridium: Rocket Lab agreed on 29 June 2026 to buy Iridium in a deal valued at about $8 billion, paying $27 a share in cash plus Rocket Lab shares, and has said it is targeting completion in mid-2027.
Losses: the Q2 net loss was $49.3M, or $0.08 a share.

Monday 9 November 2026 at 2pm Pacific, 5pm Eastern and 10pm UK time, after results are published following the US market close.
What revenue does Rocket Lab expect for Q3 2026?
Between $250M and $265M, according to its Q2 results release.
What was Rocket Lab's revenue last quarter?
$234M in Q2 2026, a record and up 62% on a year earlier.
Is Rocket Lab profitable?
Not yet. It reported a net loss of $49.3M in Q2 2026 and guided to an adjusted EBITDA loss of $17M to $23M for Q3.
